You write your domain in Rust and mark it with a handful of attributes. Undra generates idiomatic Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the schema those attributes produce, so the UI stays SwiftUI, Compose and React. Each platform keeps a local mirror of your state, so reads never cross the language boundary. A write crosses once per transaction, and the core answers with one compact binary change-set that patches every mirror. Where these pages come from. Everything here is digested from the repository: the README, the specification in docs/SPEC.md, the onboarding guide, the benchmark results and the playground app. When a page and the spec disagree, the spec wins; the repository is the record.

State in Undra lives in the Rust core as signals inside stores. Platforms hold a local mirror, reads never cross the boundary, and a write crosses once per transaction.

Everything a platform can see is one of eight kinds of thing, each declared with an attribute. They cross the boundary in one of two ways: by value (copied) or by handle (a reference to something that stays in the core). Concept Declared with Crosses Record #[undra::api] on a struct by value Enum #[undra::api] on an enum, unit or data variants by value Error #[undra::error] on an enum; adds Display and std::error::Error by value Object #[undra::api] on an impl block; methods are sync or async by handle Store an object whose struct has #[undra::store]; its signals are mirrored by handle Port #[undra::port] on a trait; implemented by the platform or by a Rust fake the core calls out to it Query, mutation #[undra::query], #[undra::mutation] on an async fn managed by the query client Function #[undra::api] on a free fn like a method with no receiver The rest of this page is about stores, because that is where reactive state lives.

A store is a struct of signals with an impl block that says what the platforms can call. The to-do list from the playground is a complete example: core/src/todos.rs #[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")] pub struct Todos { next: AtomicU64, // private state: not a signal #[undra(key = "id")] todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>, // signal 0 filter: Signal<Filter>, // signal 1 #[undra(key = "id")] visible: DerivedList<Todo>, // signal 2, a view of todos remaining: Computed<u32>, // signal 3, derived } #[undra::api(store)] impl Todos { pub fn new(ctx: Ctx) -> Self { /* … */ } pub async fn add(&self, title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError> { /* … */ } pub fn toggle(&self, id: Uuid) { /* … */ } pub fn set_filter(&self, filter: Filter) { self.filter.set(filter); } } A few rules worth knowing up front: Signals are the fields of type Signal<T>, Computed<T> and DerivedList<T>, numbered in declaration order (0, 1, 2, …). Other fields are private state: a Ctx, a counter, configuration. A store needs a constructor, a pub fn returning Self or Result<Self, E>. Generated code calls it to create the object in the core and gets back a handle. Receivers are &self. Objects are shared, so mutation goes …

A Signal<T> holds a value. You read it with get() (a clone) or with(|v| …) (a borrow), and write it with set(value) or update(|v| …). rust self.filter.set(Filter::Done); // replace self.todos.update(|list| list.retain(|t| !t.done)); // edit in place let open = self.todos.with(|list| list.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count()); A write outside a transaction is an implicit single-write transaction, so the change is committed and delivered at once. Inside update, the closure holds the value's write lock: it must not read or write the same signal, or read a computed derived from it. A violation panics with a clear message instead of deadlocking.

A Computed<T> is a value derived from signals. You name its inputs and give it a function of them: rust let parity = Computed::new(&count, |n| if n % 2 == 0 { Parity::Even } else { Parity::Odd }); let summary = Computed::new((&count, &changes), |(n, changes)| format!("{n} after {changes} changes")); Inputs are &Signal<A> or &Computed<A>, or a tuple of up to six of them, and the closure receives references. A computed is recomputed in the core, in dependency order, and pushed in the same change-set as the write that caused it. The UI never derives anything itself, so it cannot disagree with the core about, say, how many items are left. A computed list is recomputed and sent whole on every change of its inputs. For a filtered or sorted view of a keyed list, use a derived list, which costs the change instead. Because a store with computeds cannot be rebuilt from its plain signals automatically, you name a function that assembles it: #[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]. The macro tells you when you forget (E0013).

When several signals change together, group the writes. Everything inside ctx.txn commits as one transaction, so observers see one consistent change-set and never a half-applied state. The playground's counter changes two signals and derives a third: core/src/counter.rs pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) { self.ctx.txn(|| { self.count.update(|c| *c = c.saturating_add(amount)); self.changes.update(|n| *n = n.saturating_add(1)); }); // one change-set carries count, changes and parity } Transactions nest: an inner txn joins the outer one. A change-set is never split, and change-sets are delivered in commit order; for one store they reach the platform one at a time with strictly increasing transaction ids.

A platform does not receive everything. It observes signals, and only observed signals that changed are sent. Two details follow from that: Observing sends the current value right away, before the call returns in-process, so a store's initial state arrives as an ordinary change-set. A signal written while unobserved is remembered as pending and sent when someone starts observing it. Only what changed is sent. Writing filter in the to-do store ships filter and the rows that entered or left visible, and nothing else, because todos did not change. A signal marked #[undra(no_coalesce)] is delivered on every commit instead of being folded into the latest value. A change-set is a compact binary structure, described on the architecture page. For side effects that belong in the core, Effect::new(deps, f) runs f after each commit that dirtied one of its dependencies, and is cancelled when dropped.

A Signal<Vec<T>> marked #[undra(key = "field")] is a keyed list. The key is the identity of a row, and the core sends changes to it as a patch of positional operations instead of the whole list. Operation Meaning Insert { index, item } put the item at index Remove { index } take the row at index out Update { index, item } replace the row at index Move { from, to } take the row at from, then place it so it ends at to Clear empty the list The platform applies the operations in order to its own copy of the list. If a patch ever disagrees with that copy (an index out of bounds), the platform treats the signal as out of sync and observes it again, which resends the full value.

h: Why a list write costs the change, not the list
x: How the core produces the patch decides the cost. There are two ways. Recorded operations are the fast path. Signal<Vec<T>> has push, insert, remove, update_at, move_item and clear. Each one mutates the list and appends the operation it performed to a log; at commit, that log is the patch. No key is hashed and no item is compared, so the cost is the change, not the length of the list. examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs /// Inserts a new row so that it ends at `index`. One keyed `Insert`. pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> { // …check the index… let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 }); Ok(id) } Raw writes (set, update, replace) are the fallback. They are always correct, but the core cannot know what you did, so at commit it diffs the new list against what the platform has: hash every key, compare the surviving rows. That is O(list). It also falls back to sending the whole value when the two lists share no key, a key occurs twice, or more than half of the old rows were removed. The difference is measured. A DerivedList<T> is a filtered, sorted or mapped view of a keyed list, and it costs the change, not the list. You build it from the list with a pipeline: core/src/todos.rs let visible = todos.derive().filter_with(&filter, |filter, todo| filter.matches(todo)).build(); let remaining = todos.derive().filter(|todo| !todo.done).count(); // a Computed<u32> Its value is always the obvious one: the rows that pass, mapped, then sorted stably by key (filter, filter_with, map, at most one sort_by_key; equal keys keep the list's order). But it is never recomputed. It replays the list's recorded operations on an index of its own, O(log n) each, and the platform receives each as at most two patch operations: a row that enters or leaves the filter is an Insert or a Remove, a row whose sort key changes a Move and an Update (so lists animate it), a change the filter hides nothing at all. The platforms see a read-only keyed list, generated exactly like a computed list. Each platform runtime holds a mirror: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. Generated code exposes the mirror in the platform's own idiom (an @Observable property, a StateFlow, a Signal with useSignal), so reading is a local memory read that never calls into the core. Every change-set is applied on the main thread, in one hop per transaction: Swift on the MainActor, Kotlin on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and TypeScript in a queued flush on the page's main thread. A store is an object with a lifetime: release it explicitly with close() (Swift and Kotlin use deinit and a Cleaner as backstops, TypeScript a FinalizationRegistry), and UndraCore.stats() shows live handle counts.

The core can snapshot every store's plain signals (computeds are left out and recomputed) and restore them, which is how a web page recovers after a crash and how tests rebuild state. Restore keeps the same handles valid, so the platform's references keep working, and it cancels calls that were running on the stores it replaced. This is why the restore function above rebuilds computeds from signals, and why the to-do store continues its id counter above the largest id in the snapshot.

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread of its own. Time comes from the Clock port, delays from ctx.sleep (which goes through the Timer port), randomness from Rng, the network from Http. That is rule R12, and it is why every scenario can be driven with deterministic fakes in Rust and with in-memory adapters on each platform. The to-do store's ids come from a counter for the same reason. See Ports & adapters.
Data fetching, caching and offline behaviour are not something each platform reimplements. They live in the core, next to the state they feed, and every platform observes the same cache.

h: Why the data layer is in the core
x: Fetching, caching, retrying, optimistic updates and offline queues are logic, and logic is what Undra writes once. The core never opens a socket: every request goes through the Http port, which is URLSession, HttpURLConnection or fetch in an app and a scripted fake in a test. The query client keeps one cache that all platforms observe, so the to-do list on the iPhone and the one in a Chrome tab agree about what is fresh.

A query is an async fn whose first parameter is the Ctx, marked with #[undra::query]. This is the playground's remote to-do list, a GET that is cached per list: core/src/remote.rs /// The items of the server's list `list`: `GET {base}/lists/{list}/todos`. #[undra::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)] pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> { let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?; parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?) } Argument Meaning key = "…" the cache key; {param} placeholders name parameters, so two lists are two independent entries stale = "30s" how long a successful result stays fresh persist write the entry to the Kv port so it survives a restart retry = 3 how many times to retry a failed fetch idempotent (mutations) the request is safe to repeat, which makes it eligible for the offline queue The signature is checked when you compile: it must be async, take ctx: &Ctx first, and return Result<T, E>. A query whose success value is () or an Option is rejected, because a query caches a value and effects belong in a mutation (E0040 to E0042).

Platforms observe a query through a generated query handle, which is an ordinary store. For remote_todos it is RemoteTodosQueryHandle, and it has five signals: Signal Holds data the latest successful result, or nothing yet status idle, fetching, success or error error the error of the latest failed fetch, cleared by the next success fetching whether a request is in flight, also true while refetching stale data updatedAt when data last changed Constructing the handle registers an observer and starts a fetch if the entry is missing or stale. Releasing it removes the observer; when the last observer goes, the in-flight fetch is cancelled and the entry is kept for five minutes before it is garbage collected. The handle also has refetch() (fetch now, even if fresh) and invalidate() (mark stale; it refetches while observed). tsx const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox"); // observe const items = useSignal(inbox.data); // in a component const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);

An observed entry refetches when it is stale and something happens: an observer is added while it is stale, the app becomes Active again (the Lifecycle port), connectivity returns (the Connectivity port), its optional interval elapses, or it is invalidated, by key prefix. One fetch per key at a time. If five screens observe the same list, they share one in-flight request.

A failed fetch is retried retry times (three by default) with exponential backoff, min(1000 × 2ⁿ, 30000) milliseconds, with plus or minus 20% jitter. The jitter comes from the Rng port and the delay from the Timer port, so a test with fakes sees exactly the schedule it scripts.

A mutation is an async fn marked #[undra::mutation]. It shares its cache key with the query it affects. Call it through the context: rust ctx.mutate::<PostRemoteTodoMutation>((list, title)) .optimistic(move |cache| { cache.update::<RemoteTodosQuery>((cached,), |items| items.push(placeholder)); }) .invalidates(/* keys to mark stale */) .await optimistic runs inside a transaction with typed access to cache entries (get, set, update), so the UI shows the new item at once. On success the invalidates keys are marked stale and refetched if observed, which replaces the placeholder with the server's item. The playground wraps this in create_remote_todo and set_remote_done, which are what its three UIs call.

If the mutation fails, the optimistic write is undone, but only the writes that mutation made. Every cache entry carries a write stamp that changes with each write: an optimistic write, a set, or a fetch result. When a mutation fails, each entry it wrote is restored to what it was before, unless something else has written that entry since. An entry that was written since keeps that write. That rule is what makes concurrent mutations safe: a later optimistic mutation's placeholder survives an earlier mutation's rollback, even on the same entry; a fetch result that arrived in the meantime is newer than the failed closure and is kept; a later mutation that wrote directly on top of the failed one inherits its restore point, so if it fails too the entry goes back to before both. Stamps are compared, never contents, so two writes of equal data are still distinguishable. This behaviour is covered by the optimistic-rollback contract scenario on all three platforms.

A mutation marked idempotent that fails with a network error while the Connectivity port says the device is offline is not lost. It is appended to a persisted queue (the Kv key undra.query.queue2) with its parameters, the fingerprint of their types and an idempotency key, and replayed in order when connectivity returns. The request carries an Idempotency-Key header that stays the same across retries and replays, so a server can tell a repeat from a second item. rust #[undra::mutation(key = "remote-todos:{list}", idempotent)] pub async fn post_remote_todo(ctx: &Ctx, list: String, title: String) -> Result<RemoteTodo, RemoteError> { // … if let Some(key) = undra::query::idempotency_key() { request = request.with_header("Idempotency-Key", key.to_string()); } // … } A mutation that is not idempotent fails immediately when offline. While a queued call waits, the optimistic placeholder stays visible, and the caller's await keeps waiting until the network returns and the request is replayed. A queued call survives an app update: its input is migrated by parameter name, or by a #[undra::migrate] hook. One that cannot be migrated is never dropped; it moves to the dead letters, which …

Entries marked persist are written to the Kv port after each successful fetch (debounced, 250 ms) and read back when the core starts. Each entry carries the fingerprint of its type, so an unrelated change to the core keeps the cache, and an entry whose type changed is migrated by name or, if it cannot be, dropped and refetched. At most 1,000 entries are kept (set_max_persisted_entries), least recently updated first out. Storage can fail: a quota runs out, a device is locked. The Kv port reports it as a StorageError, and the client treats storage as best-effort: a failed write is logged once and retried, a failed read starts the entry empty, and an offline queue that cannot be read is never overwritten or replayed until it can be.

Because the network is a port, a query is tested with a scripted fake and no sockets. FakeHttp answers from rules and records every request, including a flaky endpoint: rust let http = FakeHttp::new(); // two timeouts, then success for ever after http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]); http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec())); Pair it with FakeClock to advance time and ScriptedConnectivity to go offline. The playground's Remote tab on every platform is this page in motion: a cached query, optimistic adds that roll back when the server refuses, and an Offline switch that queues writes and replays them on reconnect. Its source is examples/playground/core/src/remote.rs.
The core never touches the outside world directly. Time, randomness, the network, storage and the app's lifecycle all come through ports: traits the platform implements and the core calls.

A port is a Rust trait marked #[undra::port]. The platform implements it (an adapter), or a Rust fake does in a test. The core calls it through the context, for example ctx.http().request(req).await, and does not know or care what is behind it. That is what keeps the core deterministic (rule R12): it has no wall clock, no random source and no threads outside the Clock, Rng and Timer ports and the runtime. There are three kinds, and the kind decides how a call travels: Kind Meaning sync the platform answers before the call returns. A port is sync only if every method is sync async the platform answers later; the core's task waits, and can be cancelled event fire and forget from the platform into the core, such as "connectivity changed"

Port Kind Methods Clock sync now_ms() -> i64, monotonic_ns() -> u64 Rng sync fill(len) -> Bytes Log sync log(level, target, message) Http async request(HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse, HttpError> Kv async get, set, delete, list(prefix) SecureStore async the same shape as Kv, for secrets Fs async read, write, delete, list, each returning Result<_, FsError> Timer sync set(timer_id, delay_ms); the platform answers later with a timer-fired event Connectivity event changed(online, kind) with NetKind of Wifi, Cellular, Wired, Unknown or None Lifecycle event changed(state) with AppState of Active, Inactive or Background They exchange a small set of types: HttpRequest (method, url, headers, optional body, optional timeout), HttpResponse (status, headers, body), HttpError (Network, Timeout, Cancelled, InvalidUrl), Header, FsError (NotFound, Denied, Io), NetKind and AppState. These ports and types ship inside each platform runtime and are not generated into your app's bindings. Every core links undra-ports, so its schema contains them and the schema hash covers them, but the generator leaves them out and the generated code refers to the runtime's own types. An unavailable port is a normal outcome, not a bug. A port nobody registered behaves as unavailable, a call can be cancelled, and a host can reply with bytes that do not decode. The core handles all three without panicking: If the port method returns Result<T, E>, the failure becomes an E. HttpError and FsError implement From<PortError>, so an unavailable Http port is Network("the Http port has no adapter registered (E0062: register one, see ..)"), with the code and the link to the fix. Your own error type needs the same conversion, and the macro checks it at compile time (E0033). If the method has no error channel, there is no typed way to say "unavailable", so the call panics with a message that names the port and method and says how to bind one (E0062, in the shape of every diagnostic: what, why, fix, docs link). The runtime contains that panic at the boundary. Give optional ports a Result, or register them.

Mark a trait with #[undra::port]. The macro registers it in the schema and generates a proxy type, so the core calls your trait like any other, and the platform gets a protocol or interface to implement. An object travels as a parameter or a return, and nowhere else. Not allowed Why An object inside a record, a variant or a store's signal, in a stream item, a query or a mutation a value is copied, compared, saved and merged; an object is none of those. Put the object behind a method (E0064 says so) An object of another core two cores can issue the same handle numbers, so the generated code refuses it before anything is sent: UndraCallError.refused An object in a port's parameter or return pass a record or an id instead

An object a method returned is not part of a saved snapshot: after a restore (a web worker crash, undra dev reloading the core) its handle is stale, and calling the method again returns it. Constructed stores restore as before. What a store keeps in a private field is whatever its restore hook rebuilds.

Passing an object lends it. The call holds it until it finishes, so closing the wrapper while a call is in flight is safe. A failed call hands nothing out. An error, a cancel or a panic gives the references it had issued back. A shelf stays alive while you hold it, even if the core drops its own reference. By default on the main thread, in the order things happened. A callback joins the same queue as state changes, so a listener sees the stores as they were when the core called it. With background each listener has its own serial executor instead. Either way the core never runs app code inside its own call.

An implementation that throws the method's own error answers the core with it, typed. Any other error is reported through onError and the core sees the app as unavailable. A throw from a fire-and-forget method is only reported. None of it unwinds into the core. When the core stops waiting (the call that was awaiting was cancelled), the task running the implementation is cancelled too: a Swift Task, a Kotlin Job, a TypeScript AbortSignal passed as the last argument.

The core holds the callback until it lets go, so a listener you create inline lives as long as the core uses it. A core that keeps the listener and an app that keeps the core make a cycle across languages. Two ways out: A subscription object. Return something the app closes (watch above): closing it drops the core's hold. A weak wrapper. Hand the core a wrapper that forwards while the target lives and does nothing after. On the web the core is a wasm module. It can run off the main thread, and when a panic traps it, it can come back from its last snapshot.

mode: "wasm-worker" runs the core in a Web Worker, so a heavy call never blocks the UI. The core calls some ports synchronously (Clock, Rng, Log and any #[undra::port(sync)]) and cannot wait for the main thread, so those are answered in the worker. Clock, Rng and Log need nothing from you. Ports with asynchronous methods (Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs and your own async ports) run on the main thread, exactly as in wasm-main.

Put them in a small module the worker imports before the core starts, and pass its URL. The same module overrides Clock, Rng or the core's timers in this mode: ts // main.ts const core = await UndraCore.load({ mode: "wasm-worker", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, worker: { ports: new URL("./worker-ports.js", import.meta.url) }, }); // worker-ports.ts: runs inside the worker export default { [UndraIds.Ports.Locale.portId]: localePortImpl({ hello: () => "Bonjour" }), }; export const adapters = { timer: myTimer }; // optional: clock, rng, timer A synchronous port registered on the main thread in this mode is refused when the core loads (UndraError("options"), naming the port), not at its first call. With a bundler, make the module a worker entry.

A native core contains a panic and keeps going. A wasm core cannot: the panic traps the instance. With recovery: crashRecovery() (imported from @undra/runtime, so an app without it ships none of this code), the runtime keeps a snapshot of your stores (at most once a second while they change, in an idle moment, in the worker in worker mode) and restarts from it: ts import { UndraCore, crashRecovery } from "@undra/runtime"; const core = await UndraCore.load({ mode: "wasm-main", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, recovery: crashRecovery(), // or crashRecovery({ snapshotEveryMs, maxSnapshotBytes, maxRestarts, perMs }) onPanic: (report) => crashReporter.send(report), onCoreRestarted: (e) => configureRemote(core, settings), // re-apply core state that is not in a store }); On a trap What your app sees Calls and streams in flight fail with UndraCallError.Unavailable, reason restarted; they may or may not have run and are never retried for you Stores keep their handles and show the snapshot's values Query handles are created again behind the same objects, and refetch Other objects go stale: calls on them are refused Store writes after the last snapshot, running tasks and …
A wasm core needs WebCrypto. Without crypto.getRandomValues, load rejects with UndraTransportError("unsupported") rather than run with predictable idempotency keys.
An app update changes the core's types while the device still holds data the old version wrote. Undra reads it by name, converts what it can, and refuses the rest out loud.

Three things an app writes can be read by the next version of the app: a snapshot of its stores (crash recovery on the web, undra dev's reload, an app that saves one), the cached results of persist queries, and the offline queue of idempotent mutations. Each records the fingerprint of its types: a hash of exactly the records, enums and fields it holds. A change elsewhere in the core (a new method, a new query, a doc comment) does not move it, so the data is used as it is, with no work at all. When a fingerprint did change, Undra reads the old bytes with the description that was stored next to them and converts them to the new types by name. It never guesses: data that cannot be converted is refused with a typed outcome you can show, never decoded into the wrong values.

These changes need no code. They are the ones most updates are made of: Change What the old data becomes Fields or signals reordered matched by name; order is irrelevant A field added as an Option None A field added with #[undra(default)] its zero value: false, 0, "", empty, the nil UUID, the epoch A store signal added with #[undra(default)] T::default() A field, variant or signal removed dropped Enum variants added or renumbered matched by name An integer widened (i32 to i64, u8 to u32, u16 to i32), f32 to f64 the same value T to Option<T>, Bytes to Vec<u8> or back the same value Any of these inside a Vec, an Option or a map applied to every item Anything else is not structural: a narrowing (i64 to i32), a type change (i32 to String), a renamed field, variant or signal, a variant the new type no longer has, or a new field with no default. Those need a hook.

A hook is a plain function marked #[undra::migrate]. It receives the old value as a DynValue (fields and variants by name) and returns the new one, or a MigrateError to refuse it. There are three kinds: rust use undra::prelude::*; // Any persisted `Todo` whose structure changed, wherever it is. #[undra::migrate(ty = "Todo")] fn todo_from_name(old: &DynValue) -> Result<Todo, MigrateError> { let title = old.field("name").and_then(DynValue::as_str) .ok_or_else(|| MigrateError::new("a todo without a name"))?; Ok(Todo { title: title.to_owned(), done: false }) } // One signal of one store in a snapshot (`None`: the snapshot has no such signal). #[undra::migrate(store = "Profile", signal = "age")] fn age(old: Option<&DynValue>) -> Result<f32, MigrateError> { match old.and_then(DynValue::as_i64) { Some(age) if age >= 0 => Ok(age as f32), Some(age) => Err(MigrateError::new(format!("{age} is not an age"))), None => Ok(18.0), } } // The queued input of one mutation, by parameter name. #[undra::migrate(mutation = "add_todo")] fn add_todo(old: &DynRecord) -> Result<DynRecord, MigrateError> { let mut new = old.clone(); new.rename("name", "title"); Ok(new) } Structural migration is tried first, …

Each kind of data has its own refusal, and none of them loses data silently: Data Outcome A snapshot the restore fails as a whole with RestoreError::Incompatible { store, signal, reason } (restore code 7 on the platforms: UndraRestoreError / UndraRestoreException), the core is unchanged, and the reason is logged. One exception: a store type the new build removed is left out (its handles go stale) and reported. A cached query result deleted, because it can be fetched again; a WARN names the query and the reason A queued mutation never deleted: it moves to the dead letters, and the rest of the queue replays The dead letters are yours to show, export or settle: rust let query = ctx.query(); for letter in query.dead_letters() { log::warn!("{} could not be sent: {}", letter.mutation, letter.reason); // letter.params: the input by parameter name; letter.raw: the bytes as stored } query.retry_dead_letter(key)?; // after an update that added a hook query.discard_dead_letter(key); // for good ctx.query().persist_stats() counts what was migrated, dropped and dead-lettered, and the runtime's statistics carry the same numbers under query.persist.

Build the old and the new core, write the data with one and read it with the other. The playground does exactly this in its contract scenarios: UNDRA_PLAYGROUND_V2=1 undra build builds a second core whose stores, records and mutations changed the way an update does, and every platform checks that a snapshot and a queue written by the first are read by name by the second, and that an incompatible change is refused or dead-lettered. In Rust, a TestRuntime restores a snapshot you build from an edited Schema (its stores_closure is the description an older build would have written).
Most apps need one core. When a second one arrives, a vendor's SDK or a module another team ships, the two load into the same app side by side, each under its own namespace.

Put the app's domain in one core and split it into crates inside it. Add a second core only for code that ships on its own. A core's namespace names everything it exports, so two cores never collide. By default it is the core's package name in snake case; set it in undra.toml (lowercase letters, digits and _, at most 32 characters). undra.toml [core] path = "core" namespace = "acme_pay" What Named The C symbol, which returns the core's table acme_pay_undra_api iOS AcmePayCore.xcframework, one prelinked libacme_pay.a per slice Android libacme_pay.so Web acme_pay.wasm The bindings' entry, in Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript UndraAcmePay undra build refuses a namespace that a sibling project already uses, and every runtime refuses to load two cores with one. The namespace also keeps the default storage apart: each core's Kv, SecureStore, Fs and Db live under undra/<namespace>/ on every platform, so two cores that use the defaults never see each other's data unless you hand them one adapter of your own.

Load each core once, through its own entry. Every generated type defaults to the core of its own package, so a call never reaches the wrong one. Where a token lives, when it is refreshed and what logging out forgets are rules of the app, not of three UIs. Written once in the core, they hold on iOS, Android and the web.

The session is a signal. Auth.session is SignedOut or SignedIn. The root view switches on it; nothing else decides which screen shows. Tokens are secrets, not state. They go to the SecureStore port (Keychain, Android Keystore, WebCrypto) and never into a signal, because every signal is mirrored into each platform's memory. A 401 is not an error. authed adds the token and, on a 401, refreshes once and retries. A second request that meets the same 401 waits for the refresh in flight. A refresh the server refuses signs the user out, wherever the request came from. Queued writes use today's token. An offline write replayed an hour later goes through authed too, so it carries the token that is current then. Logout forgets. Both tokens, the persisted cache, the session. It is refused with a typed PendingWrites while writes wait in the offline queue: they would go out as whoever signs in next. Show the Rust core/src/auth.rs /// Who is signed in. #[undra::api] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub enum Session { /// Nobody: show the login screen. SignedOut, /// A user with a session the server accepted. SignedIn { /// The display name the server returned at sign-in. user: String, }, …

The root view switches on the session, and a failed sign-in is a case, not a string to parse. Show the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript swift struct Root: View { let auth: Auth var body: some View { switch auth.session { case .signedOut: LoginView(auth: auth) case .signedIn(let user): HomeView(user: user) } } } @MainActor func logIn(_ auth: Auth, email: String, password: String) async -> String? { do { try await auth.signIn(email: email, password: password) return nil } catch AuthError.badCredentials { return "Wrong email or password" } catch { return error.localizedDescription } } kotlin fun label(session: Session): String = when (session) { Session.SignedOut -> "Sign in" is Session.SignedIn -> session.user } suspend fun logIn(auth: Auth, email: String, password: String): String? = try { auth.signIn(email, password) null } catch (e: AuthError.BadCredentials) { "Wrong email or password" } catch (e: UndraException) { e.message } tsx export function Root({ auth }: { auth: Auth }) { const session = useSignal(auth.session); return session.kind === "signedOut" ? <Login auth={auth} /> : <Home user={session.user} />; } export async function logIn(auth: Auth, email: string, password: string): …

Sign-in puts the tokens in SecureStore and nothing in plain storage. A 401 costs exactly one refresh and the caller never sees it; a refused refresh clears both tokens, the persisted cache and the screen. A request that meets a refresh in progress waits instead of refreshing again. A session left by the last run resumes (refreshing on the way); sign-out is refused while a write is queued.

The query client has no clear() yet. Sign-out deletes the persisted entries and the recipe keys cached data by user (profile:{user}), so the next person never reads the last one's entry; in-memory entries leave with their observers. The core cannot show a login web view or an OAuth sheet: that is the platform's. It hands the code to sign_in like any other value. Source: examples/cookbook/core/src/auth.rs. The sample app, Fieldbook, uses it.
An infinite list is a keyed list that grows. The core owns the pages, the cursor and the filter, so a page crosses as one-row inserts however long the list already is.

One keyed list. posts is appended with the recorded list operations, so a page of twenty rows is twenty one-row inserts in a single change-set (SPEC 3.8), not the whole list. A derived view. visible is a DerivedList of it, filtered by topic. Typing in a search box sends the rows that entered or left the view. The cursor is a signal. Pages append until the server says there are no more, and then a scroll view's calls send nothing. A failed page keeps the cursor, so the retry continues from the same place. The core reads the file through Fs, sends it in parts through Http and shows progress as a signal. The offline queue does the retrying, so no part of the recipe asks whether the network is up.

A part is a mutation. put_part is idempotent, so while the device is offline it waits in the persisted queue and is replayed when the network returns, with the same Idempotency-Key. The upload just awaits it. Progress is a patch. uploads is a keyed list; every acknowledged part is a one-row update of sent and total, which is a progress bar. One part in the queue at a time. The queue stores a part's bytes, so memory and disk cost one part, not the file. Retry resumes. A part the server refuses fails the upload with the reason in its row. retry reads the file again and continues from the first part the server has not acknowledged. The server's name for the upload comes from the Rng port: random in an app, seeded in a test. A 150,000-byte file goes up as three parts and the screen sees 0, 64 KiB, 128 KiB, then all of it. Offline, the upload waits with one part in the queue; when the network returns it finishes, and the queue is empty. A refused second part fails the upload at 64 KiB; retry sends parts 1 and 2 and never part 0.

The Http port has no streaming body and Fs reads a file whole, so the recipe suits photos and documents, not a multi-hundred-megabyte video. The queue replays while the app runs. Undra does not yet hand an upload to the operating system's background execution (BGTaskScheduler, WorkManager). Progress is per acknowledged part, not per byte on the wire. The platform owns the socket; the core owns the policy. Which close to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are written once, in Rust, and tested with a fake clock.

One task. Live::start spawns it. It connects, reads, and when the connection ends sleeps Backoff (500 ms doubling to 30 s, jitter from the Rng port) on the Timer port, then connects again. Every end is typed. A refused upgrade with 401 or 403 stops for good, because the credentials are the problem. A normal close (1000) is a goodbye. Anything else is retried. A server that accepts and drops keeps backing off: the attempt count resets when a message arrives, not when the socket opens. Fallback. Every third failed attempt the core tries server-sent events (Fallback), resuming from the last event id, for networks that cut WebSockets. Backpressure is the core's pace. Messages are a stream the core pulls, sixteen at a time: a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one. A dropped connection shows Reconnecting and opens again after the backoff; the wait doubles while the server stays down. WebSocket and Sse are opt-in ports (WebSocket & server-sent events): the module is behind the cookbook's realtime feature. A message sent while the link is down is not queued: presence and chat are facts about now. Anything that must arrive is a mutation. A browser cannot send headers on a WebSocket, so a credential goes in the URL or a subprotocol. Source: examples/cookbook/core/src/realtime.rs.
Offline-first is three decisions the core makes once: reads come from disk, writes queue, and an update never loses what the last build left on the device.

Reads come from disk. notes is a persist query: the list is on screen from the first frame of the next launch, and refreshed in the background. The outbox is data. outbox() says how many writes wait and which ones an update could not carry over (dead letters), with the reason. An update is two rules. Build 2 renamed a field and added another. #[undra(default)] fills the new field in old data. A #[undra::migrate] hook handles the rename in cached lists and queued writes. You do not move the domain on a Monday. Undra loads next to your Kotlin and your Swift, and takes over one piece at a time.

One shared framework per module, the CocoaPods dependency, and a dev loop that rebuilds the app (KMP-9, KMP-11, KMP-13). Row ids are those of the limitations catalogue, as of October 2026. Undra's Swift output is iOS 17 by default, because a generated store is @Observable. Lower the deployment target and the same store becomes an ObservableObject: the core, the wire and the commands do not change, only how SwiftUI is told to redraw.

undra.toml [ios] deployment_target = "15.0" # 15.0 or later; below 17.0 the stores are ObservableObjects Run undra bindgen. A new app starts there with undra init todo --ios-deployment-target 15.0. [bindings] swift_observation = "observable-object" (or --swift-observation) picks the shape on any floor; "observation" with a target below 17.0 is an error that names both settings. Below iOS 16 the wire Duration is the runtime's UndraDuration (exact nanoseconds), because Swift.Duration is iOS 16.

iOS 17+ (observation) iOS 15 and 16 (observable-object) owning view @State private var todos = try! Todos() @StateObject private var todos = try! Todos() child view let todos: Todos @ObservedObject var todos: Todos environment .environment(todos) .environmentObject(todos) outside SwiftUI withObservationTracking todos.$visible.sink { … } connection state core.connection.state core.connectionObject with @ObservedObject Reading a signal is still a plain property read and a command is still a method call. The $property publishers are a gain for UIKit and Combine code on every floor.

Granularity. Observation redraws a view when a property it read changes; an ObservableObject redraws every view that observes the store when any of its properties changes. SwiftUI coalesces the events of one drain into one update. Split a big store, or observe a smaller one. A big list is copied on every patch. @Published has no in-place accessor, so a keyed patch to a list copies the array once, where Observation mutates it in place. Measured on an Apple M5 Pro (release build, 32-byte rows): about 5 µs for 1,000 rows, 48 µs for 10,000 and 0.5 ms for 100,000, against 0.2 µs at any size under Observation. It is linear in the list and paid once per applied patch, not per op (the mirror merges a frame's patches into one apply, so 100 ops cost about what 1 does). It is invisible for lists of thousands; for 100,000 rows that change every frame, page the list or observe a smaller store. One name. A store member called objectWillChange is E0051 in this mode, because ObservableObject declares it. SQLite change counts. The built-in SQLiteDbAdapter counts changes with sqlite3_changes, a C int (the 64-bit one needs iOS 15.4): a single statement that changes more than 2,147,483,647 rows …

Set deployment_target = "17.0", run undra bindgen and make the mechanical edits in the table. No core change, no wire change. The repository's examples/ios15-sample is an iOS 15.0 app over a store, a keyed list and a query; docs/IOS_15_16.md says how CI proves the floor.
A small but real app on one Rust core: field notes with photos, on the web, iOS and Android.

Fieldbook is a small but real app: field notes with photos, for a team that works where there is no signal. One Rust core, three apps (web, iOS, Android) that use only the public API, and a test suite that runs the core with no device. The cookbook's recipes, in one product.

Feature In the core Sign-in with a team code, tokens in the secure store, one re-auth on a 401 auth.rs A note is on the device before the screen shows it, and is sent when there is a network, even after a kill notes.rs: Kv, an idempotent push_note Search, tag chips, pinned first, newest first a keyed list, a DerivedList and a Computed Photos kept in the app's files and uploaded in the background Fs and the queue An update that renames a field and adds three, without losing data #[undra(default)], #[undra::migrate] Who else is in the notebook presence.rs: a reconnecting WebSocket (feature presence) State kept across a rebuild under undra dev every store has a restore function, tested

The web, iOS and Android apps build in CI (vite build, xcodebuild, assembleDebug); the screens are small on purpose. Notes are stored in Kv. The Db port (SQLite) is the next step for a notebook that grows; it is an opt-in port. One binary runs the whole loop: scaffold a project, generate bindings, build the core for each platform, serve it live, and check your machine. Every command teaches through its own help.

text undra [-C <dir>] <command> init create a new project: a core crate and an app shell per platform bindgen generate Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript bindings from the core's schema build build the core for iOS, Android, the web or this machine dev serve the core over a WebSocket to running apps, rebuilding on change doctor check toolchains and SDKs against what the project needs, with the fix for each gap adopt add an Undra core to an existing app, without touching its project files upgrade move a project to this undra's version: every pin, the bindings, the migration notes An Undra project is a directory with a undra.toml. Commands find it from the current directory upwards, or you can point at it with the global -C <dir> (long form --project-dir). undra <command> --help prints what the command does, what it needs, what it writes, and examples. Exit status is 0 on success, 1 for a failed command or a failed undra doctor, and 2 for a bad command line.

bash undra init todo # all three platforms undra init todo --platforms ios,web # only those shells undra init todo --id dev.acme.todo # application id / bundle identifier undra init todo --undra-path ~/src/undra # use a local checkout of Undra undra init todo --ios-deployment-target 15.0 # an iOS app that supports iOS 15 and 16 (ObservableObject stores) Creates a project directory with undra.toml, core/ (a working to-do store), generated/ (bindings, already generated), one minimal, real app per platform in ios/, android/ and web/, and a CI workflow (.github/workflows/undra.yml: a job for the core and one per app, installing undra at the version pinned at the top of the file). Nothing is downloaded: the templates are part of the binary. Without --undra-path the project depends on released versions of the crates and runtimes; a project that uses a checkout gets no workflow, since CI cannot see the checkout. bash undra bindgen # build the core, extract the schema, write <project>/generated undra bindgen --out ../shared/bindings undra bindgen --schema schema.json # no build: generate from a schema file undra bindgen --check # exit 1 if the generated files are stale (for CI) undra bindgen --docs # include the core's doc comments Reads the core's schema and writes the bindings the app shells import: a Swift package (<out>/swift/), a Gradle module (<out>/kotlin/) and an npm package (<out>/ts/). By default the schema comes from the core itself: the core is built as a host library, loaded, and asked for its schema. With --schema it is read from a file instead and nothing is built. Files an earlier run wrote and this one does not are removed; files you added next to them are never touched. bash undra dev # listen on 127.0.0.1:7443 undra dev --android # also adb reverse the port to every attached Android device undra dev --addr 0.0.0.0:7443 # reachable from a phone on your network undra dev --no-watch # build once and serve undra dev --no-keep-state # every rebuilt core starts fresh undra dev --record session.json # also write the session as a recording Runs the core on this machine and serves it over a WebSocket. A simulator, a phone or a browser tab connects with the remote transport and uses this core instead of a built-in one: edit Rust, save, and the core is rebuilt and restarted. The apps reconnect by themselves, with backoff, whenever the connection drops (a rebuild, a phone that slept, a restarted adb); the core's state is carried across a rebuild (it is snapshotted in this process's memory, never on disk, and restored into the new core), so an app comes back to the screen it was on and its dev bar says "Reloaded, state kept"; a changed schema, or --no-keep-state, starts the new core fresh and says so. Logs, including the development records (a line per transaction commit, port call and panic) and a line for each client that connects, reconnects or leaves, …

bash undra doctor undra doctor --platform ios undra doctor --fix # the commands that close every gap, as one block to paste (nothing is run) undra doctor --json # the report for tools Checks every prerequisite that undra init, build, dev and the device benchmarks use, and prints one line per finding. Each finding says what was found (ok, missing, or the wrong version), the value it observed, the exact fix command and the heading of docs/ONBOARDING.md that explains it. One schema feeds three generators. Three runtimes hold the mirrors. A small binary wire carries writes in and change-sets out. This page is the tour, and the specification in the repository is the contract.

Undra is a Rust core, a schema extracted from it, three code generators, and three platform runtimes. Your screens sit on generated bindings; the bindings sit on a runtime package; the runtime talks to the core through a transport that is an ABI, not a framework. Each platform has the same four layers; only the bottom one is platform-specific machinery. The core is one codebase. On each platform it is linked the way that platform expects: a prelinked static library in an XCFramework on iOS, a .so over JNI on Android, a wasm module on the web, each named after the core's namespace and reached through one table of entry points, so an app can carry more than one core. During development the same core can instead run on your machine behind a WebSocket (undra dev).

Everything is derived from the schema. Bindgen emits three trees that depend only on the matching runtime package. Everything starts with the macros. #[undra::api], #[undra::store], #[undra::port] and friends validate your code and register a description of each public type and function. Collected together, those descriptions are the schema: records, enums, objects, stores with their signals, functions, ports and queries. The CLI builds your core as a host library, loads it, asks for the schema, and hands it to undra bindgen, which writes a Swift package, a Gradle module and an npm package. Generated code depends only on the matching runtime package. Three properties of this design are worth stating plainly: Names become ids at compile time. A type id is a hash of its name, a method id a hash of Type.method, a port id a hash of port.Trait, and a signal id is its position among the store's signal fields. Every platform agrees without a registry lookup. The hash is FNV-1a. The schema has a hash. It is the FNV-1a hash of a canonical form: lists sorted by name, no whitespace, doc comments excluded, so two cores with the same public surface hash the same. Each binding carries the hash …

One mutator. The core has one lock. Whoever holds it is the core loop. A synchronous call from the host runs on the caller's thread holding that lock, so it costs a mutex acquire, not a thread hop. Async work. Async calls are tasks on a small executor with no tokio, polled by the core thread, one task per in-flight call. Cancelling a call drops its future. A blocking pool runs blocking work off the lock. It must not write signals, and debug builds refuse such writes. wasm is single threaded. The host calls undra_poll() on the next microtask whenever the core asks to be scheduled. Shutdown is orderly. Every call still in flight is answered as cancelled and every stream ends, each exactly once, before the threads are joined.

A UI and a core that were not built from the same schema must not talk. The schema hash is checked when the runtime attaches and surfaces as a typed mismatch error, and undra bindgen --check catches stale bindings at build time. Breaking the wire is a major version and needs an ADR; evolving a schema across a hash mismatch is deliberately not in v1.

Generated Swift is written the way a Swift engineer would write it by hand: value types, error enums you catch by case, async/await, AsyncSequence and an @Observable store. Swift 6 language mode, strict concurrency, no Objective-C. undra bindgen writes a Swift package (Sources/<Module>/Generated/*.swift and a Package.swift) that depends only on UndraRuntime. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.1). Reference. Every declaration the playground generates, with its docs, is in the Swift reference.

Load the core once, before any store is created, through the entry generated for it: Undra and the core's namespace ([core] namespace in undra.toml, by default the core's package name), here UndraPlaygroundCore. It checks the core's schema hash against the one the bindings were generated from and throws a clear error if they differ. UndraBootstrap.swift import UndraRuntime import PlaygroundCore @MainActor static func start() throws { let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault // URLSession, Keychain, files, … .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared) // swap one port try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters)) } In debug builds you can attach to the core that undra dev serves instead, with UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.remote(url: url, adapters: adapters)). After loading, every generated type defaults to its entry's core: try Todos() is try Todos(ctx: UndraPlaygroundCore.core). Before the core is loaded, or after shutdown(), that is a shut-down placeholder: constructors throw UndraCallError.unavailable(.closed) instead of stopping the app, and the first use logs what to do. The core links like any static library, with no -force_load, so an app can carry more than one.

The ten standard ports are implemented by UndraRuntime (URLSession, Keychain, FileManager, NWPathMonitor and so on) and are not generated into your module. Change-sets are applied on the MainActor, in one hop per transaction, so observable properties only ever change on the main thread. Stores and objects release their handle on close(), with deinit as the backstop. UndraCore.stats() exposes live handle counts for tests. Swift 6 strict concurrency is on. Generated Kotlin is what a Kotlin engineer would write by hand: data classes, sealed hierarchies, suspend functions, Flow, and StateFlows you read with collectAsState(). The runtime needs only the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines. undra bindgen writes a Gradle module (src/main/kotlin/<package>/*.kt, a build.gradle.kts and a .gitignore) that depends only on undra-runtime. It checks that the native library was built from the same schema as the bindings. A #[undra::error] becomes a sealed class extending UndraException, with the message from #[error("…")]. A generated call that can fail throws exactly one of three things: its own error, thrown as the sealed class itself, so catch (e: TodoError) and when (e) work; CancellationException, when the calling coroutine was cancelled; or UndraCallError, for anything else that went wrong with the call. The method's @throws documentation names its error. kotlin sealed class TodoError(message: String) : UndraException(message) { data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty") // a variant wrapping another error carries it: data class Http(val cause: HttpError) } viewModelScope.launch { try { store.add(draft) } catch (e: TodoError) { problem = when (e) { TodoError.EmptyTitle -> "Give it a title first." } } catch (e: UndraCallError) { problem = e.message // Panicked, Refused, Unavailable, … } // a CancellationException ends the coroutine as usual } UndraCallError is a sealed class under UndraException, so one catch (e: UndraException) shows either kind of failure to the user, and e.message reads well in a dialog. An object is a class holding a handle into the core. Sync methods that return a value are plain functions, async methods are suspend, a sync method that returns nothing is a command (it reports instead of throwing, see Errors), and stream methods return a Flow that fails with the same errors while you collect it. Signals are updated on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, in one hop per transaction. On a JVM without Android the runtime falls back to a single-thread executor, which is what the JVM test suite uses. UndraStore and UndraObject implement AutoCloseable. Call close() to release the handle (a use { } block works); a Cleaner releases leaked handles as a backstop. An object is a class holding a handle. Every method returns a Promise, which keeps the API uniform across main-thread, worker and remote modes. A command's promise resolves even when the call fails (see Errors), and a stream method returns an AsyncIterable that fails with the same errors while you iterate it. An async method takes an optional AbortSignal as its last argument to cancel the call in the core. ts export class Probe extends UndraObject { static create(core?: UndraCore): Promise<Probe>; counters(): Promise<ProbeCounters>; wait(ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<number>; ticks(count: number): AsyncIterable<number>; // backpressure through stream credit reset(): Promise<void>; // a command: never rejects } export function add(a: number, b: number): Promise<number>; Release an object with close() (idempotent) or with using where Symbol.dispose exists (Node 20+ and current browsers); a FinalizationRegistry is the backstop.

A store extends UndraStore. Every signal is a read-only Signal<T>: get() returns the current value, peek() reads without subscribing, and subscribe(fn) calls you on change and returns an unsubscribe function. Computed signals are written by the core. ts export class Todos extends UndraStore { readonly todos: Signal<Todo[]>; readonly filter: Signal<Filter>; readonly visible: Signal<Todo[]>; // computed by the core readonly remaining: Signal<number>; // computed by the core static create(core?: UndraCore): Promise<Todos>; setFilter(f: Filter): Promise<void>; // a command: never rejects add(title: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<Todo>; } Change-sets are batched with queueMicrotask into one flush per macrotask, so several signals that changed in one transaction update together and a component never renders a half-applied state.

@undra/runtime/react exports two hooks. useSignal is useSyncExternalStore over a signal, with a server snapshot. useUndra creates a store when the component mounts and closes it when it unmounts; it returns undefined until the store exists, and useSignal accepts an undefined signal. tsx import { useUndra, useSignal } from "@undra/runtime/react"; export function CounterView() { const counter = useUndra(Counter); // undefined until created const count = useSignal(counter?.count); const parity = useSignal(counter?.parity); // computed in the core, same change-set if (counter === undefined) return null; return <button onClick={() => void counter.increment()}>{count} ({parity})</button>; } Adapters ship for the other frameworks as thin files, exported from @undra/runtime/vue (useSignal as a shallowRef, useUndra), /svelte (signalStore, a Readable) and /solid (useSignal as an Accessor, useUndra). The frameworks are optional peer dependencies; the core package imports none of them.

The runtime is testable without a browser: over the remote transport against a native core, and against a WAT stub of the wasm ABI. The contract suite runs the same scenarios as the Swift and Kotlin runners, against the real wasm module.
Structured local data with SQLite, written once in the core. The platform owns the file and the thread; the core sends bound statements and gets typed rows back.

Db is an opt-in port over the SQLite each platform already has: the system library on iOS, android.database.sqlite on Android, a JDBC driver on the JVM, node:sqlite in Node and wa-sqlite in a worker on the web. The core stays small and never blocks: the platform owns the database and its thread. On the web the files live in the origin private file system, which one tab holds at a time: a second tab of the same app gets Unavailable. core/Cargo.toml [dependencies] undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["db"] }

Migrations are numbered SQL. The platform runs every one the database has not seen yet, in one transaction: if one fails, none of them happened. core/src/notes.rs const MIGRATIONS: &[Migration] = &[ Migration::new(1, "CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"), Migration::new(2, "CREATE INDEX notes_done ON notes (done)"), ]; let db = Database::open(&ctx, "notes", MIGRATIONS).await?;

SQL is a &'static str, so a value can only reach a statement as a bound parameter. Cells come back typed. rust db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?; let rows = db.query("SELECT id, title, done FROM notes WHERE done = ?", params![false]).await?; for row in rows.iter() { let id: i64 = row.get("id")?; let title: String = row.get("title")?; }

A transaction commits when its body returns Ok and rolls back on Err, or when its task is dropped half-way. rust db.transaction(|tx| async move { for title in titles { tx.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?; } Ok(()) }).await?;

Error When Constraint { kind, .. } a UNIQUE, NOT NULL, foreign-key or CHECK constraint failed Busy the database stayed locked past five seconds Migration { version, .. } a migration failed and everything rolled back, or the file is newer than the app Sql a syntax error, a missing table, a cell read as the wrong type Corrupt, Full, Unavailable the file, the disk, or no database to talk to

FakeDb answers by SQL fragment, injects failures and records every statement, migration and transaction, so the core's database logic is tested without a device. rust fakes.db.fail_on("INSERT", DbError::Full); assert_eq!(notes.add("milk".into()).await, Err(DbError::Full)); Design: ADR-048.
Live data comes into the core like everything else: through a port. The core reads at its own pace and decides when to reconnect; the platform owns the socket.

WebSocket and Sse are opt-in ports: a core asks for them with a cargo feature, and a core that does not keeps the schema hash and the wasm size it had. Each platform answers with its own client: URLSessionWebSocketTask, the Kotlin runtime's client on the JVM and Android, the browser's WebSocket. core/Cargo.toml [dependencies] undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["websocket", "sse"] }

The core connects, sends and reads. Messages arrive as a stream the core pulls: it asks for 16 at a time, so a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one. core/src/chat.rs use undra::ports::ws::{WsConnection, WsError, WsMessage, WsOptions}; let conn = WsConnection::connect(&ctx, "wss://chat.example.com/room", WsOptions::default()).await?; conn.send_text("hello").await?; let mut messages = conn.messages(); while let Some(next) = undra::ports::next(&mut messages).await { match next { Ok(WsMessage::Text(text)) => room.push(text), Ok(WsMessage::Binary(_)) => {} Err(WsError::Closed { code: 1000, .. }) => break, // the server said goodbye Err(error) => return Err(error), } }

What happened The stream ends with the core called close nothing: it simply ends the server sent a close frame Closed { code, reason } the connection dropped Network the server broke the protocol Protocol the upgrade was refused Refused { status } (from connect) Browsers cannot send headers with a WebSocket, so the browser adapter refuses a connect that has some instead of dropping them: put the credential in the URL or a subprotocol.

The port never reconnects on its own: which close codes to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are your app's rules, and they run in the core, where a test drives them with a fake clock. Backoff gives the delay, a weak context sleeps. rust let backoff = Backoff::default(); // 500 ms doubling to 30 s, with jitter from the Rng port let mut attempt = 0; while weak.sleep(backoff.delay(attempt, &*ctx.rng())).await.is_ok() { attempt += 1; // connect again, re-subscribe, reset `attempt` once a message arrives }

sse::subscribe is a stream of events parsed as the HTML standard says. It ends with Ended when the server finishes the response; subscribe again with the last event id to resume. rust let mut events = sse::subscribe(&ctx, "https://api.example.com/feed", vec![], last_id.clone()); while let Some(Ok(event)) = undra::ports::next(&mut events).await { last_id = event.id.clone().or(last_id); feed.apply(event.data); }

FakeWebSocket and FakeSse are scripted servers: accept or refuse, push, close, drop, echo. They record what the core sent and how much it pulled, so backpressure is an assertion. rust let fakes = fakes::install(&t); fakes.web_socket.echo(true); // ... the core connects and sends ... assert!(fakes.web_socket.delivered(conn) <= consumed + 24); On the web the adapters are an opt-in import, @undra/runtime/realtime, so an app that does not use them ships none of them. Design: ADR-047.

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: Every cross-language framework has to decide what crosses the boundary, how often, and what it costs. Undra's answer fits in a sentence: reads never cross the boundary, and writes cross once per transaction. This post walks through the mechanism with real generated code from the playground app, the numbers we measured with links to the raw results, and an honest section on what the design costs you. 30 Sep 2026 · 14 min read · Undra team

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: There are roughly three ways to keep native UI in step with state that lives in another language. The UI can ask for each value when it needs it, which costs a crossing per read per render. The core can send the whole state after every change, which costs a crossing proportional to the state. Or the UI can hold a copy, and the core can send only what changed. Undra does the third, and states it as the fifth rule of its constitution: reads never cross the boundary; writes cross once per transaction; no generated getter calls into the core. The UniFFI and Crux comparison looks at how other tools place themselves among these options. There is a second reason for the rule besides speed. If reads crossed, a core in a web worker or behind a WebSocket during undra dev would need every read to be asynchronous. Because reads are local, the same generated API works in-process, in a worker and over a socket.

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: A write is a call. The runtime encodes the arguments, takes a call id, and crosses the boundary once. The core runs the method, and everything it writes inside one transaction is committed together. The counter store in the playground shows the idea: Playground code, reformatted: examples/playground/core/src/counter.rs pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) { self.ctx.txn(|| { self.count.update(|count| *count = count.saturating_add(amount)); self.changes.update(|changes| *changes = changes.saturating_add(1)); }); // one change-set carries count, changes and the computed parity } On commit the core recomputes the dirty computed values in dependency order, then builds one change-set for each store the transaction touched, containing only signals that the platform has observed and that changed. p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread outside the runtime. Time comes from the Clock port, delays from the Timer port, randomness from Rng, the network from Http. That is rule R12. The to-do store shows the discipline: its item identities come from a counter, not from a random source, and after a restore the counter continues above the largest identity in the snapshot. The payoff is testability. In Rust, TestRuntime installs deterministic fakes for every port, including a FakeClock that fires timers when you advance it, and runs the executor on the test thread. On each platform, the contract tests supply a manual clock and an in-memory HTTP server. Scenario S12 advances the clock by 31 seconds to prove that a cached query becomes stale and refetches, without waiting 31 seconds. This is determinism of inputs. It does not make native thread scheduling deterministic, and we do not claim replayability beyond what the tests exercise.

x: Every design has a price, and the honest version of this post lists it. Memory for copies. An observed keyed list exists in the core, in a baseline copy the core keeps to build patches against, and in the platform mirror. A computed value is sent whole and held in the mirror too. If you observe a large keyed list, you pay for three copies of it. Derived lists cross whole. Only a keyed Signal<Vec<T>> gets patches. A Computed<Vec<T>> like visible crosses as a full value whenever it changes, so for a large list, derive the filtered view on the platform from the keyed source instead. A crossing per write. Writes are calls: they encode arguments, cross, and run under the core's single lock. A long synchronous method blocks other callers, so long work belongs in an async method. Every TypeScript method returns a Promise. The O(change) path is opt-in. The recorded list operations are what make patches cheap. A raw update closure is correct and O(list). The discipline of a schema. Every public type exists in the schema or it does not cross. Names become ids, so renaming a method changes the wire. p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: Undra and Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) both let you write your domain logic once and keep the screens in SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose and React. They bet on different languages, boundaries and toolchains. We build Undra, so read this with that in mind: every statement about KMP is dated to 30 September 2026 and linked to its source, and one section covers when KMP is the better choice. 30 Sep 2026 · 13 min read · Undra team How to read this page. Statements about KMP describe its state on 30 September 2026 and link to JetBrains' or Google's documentation where one exists. We have not benchmarked KMP and make no numeric claims about it. If something is wrong or has moved, open an issue and we will correct the page with a dated note.

p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: KMP compiles Kotlin to each target: the JVM and Android, native code for iOS, JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web. Your shared code is Kotlin, it runs in a Kotlin runtime on every platform, and platform code calls into it. Undra compiles Rust to a C ABI library (iOS, and Android through JNI) and to a wasm module (web), and generates Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from a schema extracted from the Rust. Platform code does not call into your logic to read state; it holds a local mirror. Three differences follow: Language. Kotlin or Rust. For an Android-first team Kotlin is already the daily language. Rust gives you a borrow checker and no garbage collector, and asks more of the people learning it. Boundary. In KMP, platform code reads shared state by calling into the Kotlin runtime. In Undra, reads are local and only writes cross, once per transaction. Scope. KMP is broader: share only logic, or logic and UI with Compose Multiplatform. Undra never shares UI, and ships the state and data layer that KMP leaves to libraries.

p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: If you have decided your logic lives in Rust, there are at least three serious ways to get it under a SwiftUI, Compose or React app: UniFFI, which generates bindings and stops there; Crux, which adds an architecture; and Undra, which adds reactive state, a data layer and a dev loop. p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: UniFFI owns the crossing: it generates the foreign-language side of a Rust library's API. Crux owns the shape of the app: an Elm-style core that never does I/O and a thin shell that does. Undra owns the state that sits between core and screen: signals the UI observes, a data layer, and the loop for developing both. You can stop at any layer. A small Rust library with a handful of functions needs UniFFI and nothing else. An app whose state you want to reason about as a pure function of events may want Crux. Undra is for apps where the hard part is keeping native UI consistent with stateful, server-backed logic on three platforms. Undra does not build on UniFFI or Crux: it has its own wire format and a fixed 19-function C ABI, so nothing below is a statement that one is built on another.

x: UniFFI is Mozilla's toolkit for generating foreign-language bindings for Rust libraries (project). p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: Crux, maintained by Red Badger, splits an app into a Core in Rust and a Shell in the platform's language (project). The core follows the Elm architecture. You define an Event enum, a Model, a ViewModel and an Effect type, and an update function from event and model to a Command that requests effects. The core never performs I/O. It describes the work as data, the shell performs it and hands the outcome back, and the core continues. A shell is therefore a small loop: send an event, perform each requested effect and resolve it, and read the view model when a render is requested. Its README states that Crux is pre-1.0 and production-ready, with occasional breaking changes, and it links engineering write-ups from Proton and Photoroom. x: This is the deepest architectural difference between Crux and Undra, so it deserves care. In Crux the shell renders a ViewModel. When the core asks for a render, the shell calls view() and receives the whole view model, serialised across the boundary. That is a clean contract: the UI is a function of one value, consistency is trivial, and the view model is easy to assert on in tests. The cost scales with the size of the view model, not the size of the change, and the shell must work out what changed, which SwiftUI and React already do by diffing. For a settings screen this is unremarkable. For a long list that changes one row at a time, the work per update is proportional to the list. Crux is not stuck there. Photoroom's engineering blog describes running into this with a large view model, where the UI could not tell what had changed, and building patches on top: key-path changes generated by diffing view models before and after an update, and sending only those (Photoroom, part 3). In Crux that is something you build; in Undra it is the built-in model. In Undra the state that crosses is per signal, and each platform observes the signals it renders. h: When UniFFI is the better choice
x: You want bindings, not a framework. If you have a Rust library and need Swift and Kotlin callers, UniFFI is smaller and simpler to adopt than anything that also brings a runtime. You already have state management on each platform. If each app has its own architecture and you want to move only the computation, a generator of call bindings fits without asking you to adopt mirrors or signals. Your API is objects and callbacks. UniFFI exposes Rust objects with methods, supports callback interfaces and foreign traits, and maps async Rust functions to each language's native futures. Undra's surface is stores, records, methods and ports. You need other languages. Python and Ruby are in the tree and third-party generators cover Go, C# and more. Undra targets Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. You want the longer track record. It is used extensively in Firefox and maintained by Mozilla. Undra is a new v1.0. Your surface is small. A few functions do not need schema-driven stores.

h: When Crux is the better choice
x: You want Elm's discipline. Every state change is an event, the core is a pure function of events and resolved effects, and tests are plain Rust with no fakes. Some teams find that the most maintainable way to build an app, and Undra does not impose it. Your view models are small and whole-state updates are fine. Then Crux's single-value contract is simpler than signals and patches. You want Rust on the web side too. Crux supports Rust web shells such as Leptos and Yew and lets a Rust shell import the core directly. You need a C# shell. Crux's README says its FFI layer is generated across native, web and C# shells. Undra targets Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. You want a community with production stories. Crux's README links write-ups from Proton and Photoroom. Undra has a reference app and a test suite, not production mileage. You do not need a built-in data layer. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Cross-platform tools fall into two camps. One shares the pixels: you write the UI once and a toolkit puts it on every platform. The other shares what is under the pixels and lets each platform draw its own screens. Undra is in the second camp, and this post explains why without pretending the first camp is wrong. Shared UI is the right answer for many products, and we say which. 30 Sep 2026 · 9 min read · Undra team How to read this page. We build Undra, a framework that shares logic and never UI, so we have a stake in this argument. Statements about Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform describe them on 30 September 2026 and link to their own documentation. If you think we have misrepresented one, open an issue.

p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The first bet is that the UI is the expensive part, so share it. Three mature tools make this bet in different ways. Flutter has its own rendering engine, Impeller, and its own implementations of each UI control rather than deferring to the system's (architecture overview). You write Dart, and Flutter paints its own widgets with its own engine. React Native turns a tree of React components into the platform's own views: a UIView on iOS, an android.view.ViewGroup or android.widget.TextView on Android (render pipeline). You write JavaScript or TypeScript and the screen is made of host views. Its New Architecture has been the default since React Native 0.76 (docs). Compose Multiplatform takes Jetpack Compose to other platforms. JetBrains lists iOS as Stable and web as Beta and describes interop that lets you keep existing SwiftUI or Android View code (product page). Its FAQ says the components are drawn on a canvas rather than being platform widgets (FAQ). The second bet is that the logic is the expensive part, so share that and keep the UI native.
