p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The benefits are large and we do not want to undersell them. One UI codebase. One set of screens, one set of UI tests, one design system implementation. A small team ships to several platforms with the headcount of one. Consistency by construction. The same screen behaves the same way everywhere, which matters when the product's identity is its own look and not the platform's. Iteration speed. These toolkits put a lot of effort into fast feedback loops for UI work, and a single codebase means a fix lands everywhere at once. Fit with your existing skills. A team that already writes React can reach mobile through React Native. A Kotlin team can reach iOS through Compose Multiplatform. Shared UI is usually the right choice when any of these describes the product: A small team or a startup that needs to reach several platforms quickly. A brand-led or highly custom interface, where a bespoke look matters more than platform convention. An internal tool or a content app where the screens are simple and the platform's idioms are not a selling point. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The trade is not the same for each toolkit, and none of it is fatal. It is a set of costs that show up at the edges, and the costs are different if you start from a native app than if you start from nothing. Platform idioms. Native controls bring platform behaviour with them: text selection, scroll physics, navigation transitions, keyboard handling, system sheets and menus. React Native inherits much of this because its screens are host views. Flutter and Compose Multiplatform draw their own controls, so matching a platform convention is the toolkit's work, or yours. Brand-led apps often do not want a match, which is the point of the first bet. Day-one OS features. When a platform ships a new UI API, native code can adopt it with the new SDK. A shared toolkit adopts it on its own schedule, or you embed a native view. Flutter documents platform views for exactly this, and notes that synchronising them with Flutter's rendering carries overhead, so it recommends them for complex controls where reimplementing is impractical. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Undra draws the line exactly at the UI. Everything under it is shared: domain logic, reactive state, the data layer, persistence and the dev loop. Everything above it stays a hand-written SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose or React screen. Our reasoning starts from where the work repeats. In our experience the code beneath the UI is where the three platforms disagree and where the subtle bugs live: the cache, the retry policy, the offline queue, pagination, the session refresh. Teams write these three times and get three slightly different answers. The screens, by contrast, are where platform expertise pays off. So Undra shares the part that must be identical and leaves the part that should feel native. The bar is that a SwiftUI view bound to Undra state is indistinguishable from one bound to Swift state. That is achievable because the generated store is an ordinary @Observable class, a Kotlin StateFlow or a TypeScript Signal. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
h: Why not share the UI too?
x: We considered it and rejected it, for a reason that is about focus more than principle. Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform are whole-UI products, each maintained by a large team that chases every platform's new UI features, keeps accessibility in step and polishes rendering. An Undra UI toolkit would be a smaller and later version of one of them, and it would be the part of Undra most likely to age badly. The moment a framework paints pixels on three platforms it takes on that ongoing work, and it inherits the trade-offs listed above. There is also a practical reason. If the UI stays native, Undra's generated code has a clear bar to meet: a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer who has never seen Rust must be able to review it and find it idiomatic. The golden files that lock the generated output are how the project holds itself to that bar.

p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Drawing the line here has costs, and they are the mirror image of what shared UI buys. You build three UIs. That means three implementations of the design, three UI test suites, and keeping the screens from drifting apart. If your product needs pixel-identical screens, this is the wrong tool. You need Rust. The core is Rust. Undra's macros emit errors that say what, why, how to fix it and where to read more, and they keep lifetimes and threads off the common path, but the borrow checker remains, and in our experience most mobile teams have few Rust engineers. Only the people writing the core need it; the platform teams consume generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. Logic must be worth sharing. If your app is mostly UI with little logic beneath it, sharing the logic buys little. The worst case for Undra is an app that is 90 percent UI and 10 percent logic. It is a new framework.
